outline.title: Introducing DP-3T: Decentralized, Privacy-Preserving
outline.content: Explaining the core principles of DP-3T (Decentralized Privacy-Preserving Proximity Tracing). Emphasizing its decentralized nature and commitment to user privacy as key differentiators.
outline.example: DP-3T offers a smarter way. Instead of sending all your location data to a central server, your phone only shares anonymous 'keys' when you test positive. Think of it like a secure digital whisper network, not a public announcement board.

outline.title: The Technology: Bluetooth & Cryptographic Keys
outline.content: Diving into the technical underpinnings. Explaining how Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) is used for proximity detection and how ephemeral cryptographic keys (Temporary Contact Keys - TCKs) are generated and exchanged. Visualizing the concept of random, short-lived keys.
outline.example: Your phone constantly broadcasts tiny signals, like a friendly wave, using Bluetooth. When it 'waves' at another phone nearby, both phones record a unique, temporary digital handshake – a TCK. These TCKs are like secret codes that change every few minutes. This visual shows two phones exchanging these temporary codes.

outline.title: How It Works: Reporting and Infection Status
outline.content: Illustrating the step-by-step process when a user tests positive. Focusing on how TCKs are uploaded to a shared server and how other users' devices can securely download and check these TCKs without revealing personal information.
outline.example: If 'Alice' tests positive, her phone uploads a list of all the TCKs it generated in the last two weeks to a public server. 'Bob's' phone then downloads this list. Bob's phone checks if any of the TCKs on the server match the TCKs *it* generated. If there's a match, it means Bob was near Alice's phone. The app then alerts Bob anonymously to get tested. This animation shows Alice's phone sending encrypted codes, and Bob's phone checking them.

outline.title: The Privacy Guarantee: Data Minimization and Anonymity
outline.content: Reinforcing the privacy protections. Explaining why TCKs are ephemeral, how they don't reveal location or identity, and the role of data minimization in DP-3T's design. Comparing this to centralized approaches.
outline.example: Critically, Bob's phone never knows *who* generated those TCKs. It only knows that *some* phone that was near it generated them. The TCKs are like disposable anonymity masks. This prevents tracking Bob's movements or identifying Alice. Unlike systems that know 'Alice was at this cafe at 2 PM,' DP-3T only knows 'Bob was near an infected individual at some point.'

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]

        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2

section_1.title: The Challenge: Contact Tracing and Privacy
section_1.content: Understanding the critical role of contact tracing in controlling infectious disease outbreaks. Highlighting the inherent privacy concerns with traditional methods and centralized digital solutions.
section_1.example: Imagine a town facing a sudden flu outbreak. To stop its spread, we need to identify everyone who came into contact with infected individuals. Historically, this involved manual interviews and spreadsheets, which were slow and raised privacy issues about who knew what about whom. Modern apps tried to improve this but often collected too much personal data.

section_2.title: Introducing DP-3T: Decentralized, Privacy-Preserving
section_2.content: Explaining the core principles of DP-3T (Decentralized Privacy-Preserving Proximity Tracing). Emphasizing its decentralized nature and commitment to user privacy as key differentiators.
section_2.example: DP-3T offers a smarter way. Instead of sending all your location data to a central server, your phone only shares anonymous 'keys' when you test positive. Think of it like a secure digital whisper network, not a public announcement board.

section_3.title: The Technology: Bluetooth & Cryptographic Keys
section_3.content: Diving into the technical underpinnings. Explaining how Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) is used for proximity detection and how ephemeral cryptographic keys (Temporary Contact Keys - TCKs) are generated and exchanged. Visualizing the concept of random, short-lived keys.
section_3.example: Your phone constantly broadcasts tiny signals, like a friendly wave, using Bluetooth. When it 'waves' at another phone nearby, both phones record a unique, temporary digital handshake – a TCK. These TCKs are like secret codes that change every few minutes. This visual shows two phones exchanging these temporary codes.

section_4.title: How It Works: Reporting and Infection Status
section_4.content: Illustrating the step-by-step process when a user tests positive. Focusing on how TCKs are uploaded to a shared server and how other users' devices can securely download and check these TCKs without revealing personal information.
section_4.example: If 'Alice' tests positive, her phone uploads a list of all the TCKs it generated in the last two weeks to a public server. 'Bob's' phone then downloads this list. Bob's phone checks if any of the TCKs on the server match the TCKs *it* generated. If there's a match, it means Bob was near Alice's phone. The app then alerts Bob anonymously to get tested. This animation shows Alice's phone sending encrypted codes, and Bob's phone checking them.

section_5.title: The Privacy Guarantee: Data Minimization and Anonymity
section_5.content: Reinforcing the privacy protections. Explaining why TCKs are ephemeral, how they don't reveal location or identity, and the role of data minimization in DP-3T's design. Comparing this to centralized approaches.
section_5.example: Critically, Bob's phone never knows *who* generated those TCKs. It only knows that *some* phone that was near it generated them. The TCKs are like disposable anonymity masks. This prevents tracking Bob's movements or identifying Alice. Unlike systems that know 'Alice was at this cafe at 2 PM,' DP-3T only knows 'Bob was near an infected individual at some point.'

section_6.title: DP-3T in Action: Real-World Applications & Future
section_6.content: Briefly touching upon the adoption and effectiveness of DP-3T or similar protocols in public health initiatives. Discussing the ongoing evolution of privacy-preserving technologies.
section_6.example: Many countries implemented contact tracing apps based on DP-3T principles. While challenges exist, these systems demonstrated a powerful way to balance public health needs with fundamental privacy rights. Imagine a digital guardian for your health, only alerting you when necessary, and always respecting your digital footprint.
